where

\beta_i: The noise schedule, defined in the Definitions section below.
\mu_\theta, \sigma_i^2: The learned reverse step’s mean and its pre-fixed variance.
\alpha_i: \alpha_i = 1 - \beta_i, the fraction of the previous state’s variance retained at step i.
\bar\alpha_i: The cumulative product, \bar\alpha_i = \prod_{j \le i}(1-\beta_j).
\epsilon_\theta: The network’s noise estimate.
f, g: The forward SDE’s drift and diffusion coefficients — not the transform f of Part 2.
s_\theta(x,t): The estimated score \nabla_x \log p_t.
d\bar W: The increment of a reverse-time Brownian motion — the reverse-time SDE is post #3’s subject.
\mu(t), \Sigma(t): The kernel mean factor and covariance — the kernel mean is \mu(t)\,x_0 — which solve linear ODEs in f and g.
\lambda(t): \lambda : [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}_{>0}, a positive weighting function.
SGD: Stochastic gradient descent.
PF-ODE: The probability-flow ODE (ordinary differential equation).
Ancestral sampling: Sampling the learned reverse steps in sequence, i = N, \ldots, 1 — the procedure of the Sampling subsection below.
Reverse diffusion: A discretization of the reverse-time SDE, taking one noisy step per time increment.
Predictor-Corrector (PC): A reverse-time-SDE step followed by score-based corrector steps at the same noise level.
Invertible PF-ODE latent: The ODE is deterministic and reversible, so each x_0 maps to a unique endpoint that maps back to it; that endpoint serves as a latent code, and the change-of-variables formula along the flow turns it into an exact \log p_\theta(x_0).

Each stochastic gradient step samples a fresh triple: a data point x_0 \sim p_0, a step index i (uniform over 1,\dots,N) or a time t (uniform over [0,1]), and a noise vector \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I).

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
4.3 Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models
Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) [2] are discrete-time diffusion models with roots in nonequilibrium thermodynamics. Like other diffusion models they generate new samples through one central idea: learn to undo noise. If a model can take a slightly noisy sample and remove a small amount of the noise, then, starting from pure noise and applying this repeatedly, it recovers a clean sample (Figure 12).








Figure 12: DDPM as a pair of Markov chains. The forward process, with transitions p(x_i \mid x_{i-1}) (top, fixed), adds Gaussian noise until x_N is pure noise. The reverse Markov chain, with learned reverse steps q_\theta(x_{i-1} \mid x_i) (bottom), denoises back to data. Training fits the reverse Markov chain to invert the forward process.






4.3.1 Forward process (noising)
A fixed, parameter-free procedure that takes a data sample x_0 \sim p_0 and progressively adds Gaussian noise to it, producing a sequence x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_N in which each x_i is a noisier version of x_{i-1} and the endpoint x_N is close to pure noise — a sample from a fixed, data-independent distribution (Figure 13). How much noise enters at each step is set by a noise schedule. This forward process is not an analogy to a diffusion; it is one.








Figure 13: The forward (noising) process, illustrated on a 2-D toy dataset (two interleaving moons, standardized). Left to right, progressively more Gaussian noise is mixed into each sample; the two-moon structure dissolves until, at the final step, the points are indistinguishable from a sample from a standard Gaussian \mathcal{N}(0, I) — the fixed, data-independent distribution the reverse process starts from. Colours mark the two moons, showing how all structure is erased.





The forward process yields two outputs: for training, clean–noised sample pairs; for inference, pure noise.


4.3.2 Reverse process (denoising)
A learned procedure, usually implemented using neural networks, that starts from pure noise and removes noise step by step, running the forward process in reverse to produce a new sample from p_0. As shown in the table above, each learned reverse step is modeled as a Gaussian distribution whose variance is fixed beforehand, and the only entity to predict is its mean \mu_\theta. Reparameterizing converts the mean-prediction problem into a noise-prediction problem, and \epsilon_\theta is what the network learns to predict. Once the \epsilon_\theta estimate is in hand, \mu_\theta is computed deterministically. That mean, along with the pre-fixed \sigma_i, is used to sample a slightly denoised version of its input. Each reverse step is trained to invert the corresponding forward step. On a training pair the final step x_1 \to x_0 is fitted to return that training sample. At sampling time the same chain, started from a fresh noise sample, produces a new x_0, which is what generation needs.
Note that during actual training, instead of N sequential steps, i is fed to the network as an input, so a single network represents all N reverse steps and each gradient step trains one of them at random. The sequencing lives in the conditioning, not in a loop.


4.3.3 Sampling
The forward process is set up so that x_N has a known, simple distribution we can sample from directly — a standard Gaussian in this case. To generate new data, we sample a noise vector from this distribution and run the reverse process: if the network has learned to undo a single step of the noising process, applying those steps in sequence turns noise into data.
Note that during sampling, unlike training, we take N sequential steps i = N, N-1, \ldots, 1. At each step, the current x_i and i are fed to the network, which outputs the estimated noise \epsilon_\theta for that step. Like training, that \epsilon_\theta is used to compute \mu_\theta, and this, along with the fixed \sigma_i, is used to generate a slightly denoised sample from this estimated Gaussian distribution.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
section: 4.4 Why convert the discrete DDPM forward process into an SDE
text:
4.4 Why convert the discrete DDPM forward process into an SDE
Before getting into how the DDPM forward process becomes an SDE, and how that yields the closed-form perturbation kernel, it is worth asking why the conversion is needed at all. DDPM obtains that kernel directly, by composing Gaussians and induction on the step index. For that one result the discrete argument is shorter, and nothing below improves on it.
The continuous-time route is taken for what it makes available beyond it. The integrating-factor transform applies to any linear SDE, so it yields the perturbation kernel for the Variance-Exploding schedule (post #3), and for any other linear-SDE noise schedule, without repeating the argument — whereas the induction depends on the particular way the Variance-Preserving steps compose.
The SDE is also the object the rest of the theory relies upon: the Fokker-Planck equation, the reverse-time SDE, and the probability-flow ODE with its numerical solvers all start from the continuous-time process, and none of them follows from the inductively obtained kernel.
And it is the same transform already applied to the OU process in Part 2 — the sense in which one lemma serves both derivations.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
4.5 Definitions
As discussed in the above section, DDPM is natively discrete, so to convert it to a continuous-time process, we pick the unit interval [0, 1] and divide it into N equal intervals of size 1/N. This maps N discrete steps i = 1, 2, \ldots, N to N time-steps t = 1/N, 2/N, \ldots, 1. As the final step, we take the step count N \to \infty so the per-step time shrinks to an infinitesimal dt and the sequence becomes an SDE. This is why each object below carries two labels: a discrete one indexed by the step number, and a continuous one indexed by time.

Partition (N, \Delta t, \tau_i):

N: The number of steps.
i: The step index, i \in \{0, 1, \ldots, N\}.
t: The continuous time, t \in [0, 1].
\Delta t: The step size, \Delta t = 1/N.
\tau_i: The continuous time corresponding to step i, \tau_i = i/N.

Data sample x_0: A clean sample from the data distribution, x_0 \sim p_0, with x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^d.
State x_i / x_t:

The partially-noised version of x_0.
x_i \in \mathbb{R}^d in discrete time; x_N is the noisiest state.
x_t \in \mathbb{R}^d in continuous time; x_{t=1} is the noisiest state (written with the time explicit, since x_1 denotes the first discrete state).

Noise schedule:

Noise added at each step, fixed in advance, not learned.
\beta_i: The discrete per-step noise variance, \beta_i \in (0, 1) for i = 1, \ldots, N.
\beta(t): The continuous-time noise-variance rate, a continuous function \beta : [0, 1] \to (0, \infty) — over an interval dt the injected noise has variance \beta(t)\, dt.
\alpha_i: Defined as \alpha_i = 1 - \beta_i, the fraction of the previous state’s variance retained at step i.

Cumulative product \bar\alpha_i / \bar\alpha(t):

It is the fraction of the original data variance still present at step i in the discrete case and time t in the continuous case.
\bar\alpha_i: The discrete cumulative product \bar\alpha_i := \prod_{s=1}^{i} \alpha_s.
\bar\alpha(t): The continuous cumulative product \bar\alpha(t) := \exp\!\big(-\!\int_0^t \beta(s)\, ds\big).

Injected noise:

\epsilon_i: The noise added at step i, \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) i.i.d., independent of x_0.
\epsilon: The standardized accumulation of the injected noise — the total noise in x_i equals \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_i}\,\epsilon in distribution, with \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) (a different such variable for each i).

Forward transition p(x_i \mid x_{i-1}):

The conditional distribution of x_i given x_{i-1}:  p(x_i \mid x_{i-1}) = \mathcal{N}\!\big(x_i;\ \sqrt{1 - \beta_i}\, x_{i-1},\ \beta_i I\big) 
It transforms x_{i-1} into x_i by contracting the previous state by \sqrt{1 - \beta_i} and adding Gaussian noise of variance \beta_i.
Equivalently, in reparameterized form:  x_i = \sqrt{1 - \beta_i}\, x_{i-1} + \sqrt{\beta_i}\, \epsilon_i 
The whole forward process is the chain of these transitions.

Discrete perturbation kernel p(x_i \mid x_0):

The conditional distribution of the noised state given x_0, obtained by composing the forward transitions and marginalizing out the intermediate states — Gaussian in closed form, derived by induction in Appendix A.7:  p(x_i \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\!\big(x_i;\ \sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}\, x_0,\ (1 - \bar\alpha_i) I\big) 
It produces x_i from x_0 directly by scaling the data by \sqrt{\bar\alpha_i} and adding Gaussian noise of variance 1 - \bar\alpha_i.
Equivalently, in reparameterized form:  x_i = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_i}\, \epsilon  which lets us sample x_i for any i without iterating through the intermediate steps.

Continuous perturbation kernel p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0):

The continuous-time counterpart, likewise Gaussian in closed form, derived with Itô’s lemma in Section 4.9:  p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\!\big(x_t;\ \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0,\ (1 - \bar\alpha(t)) I\big) 
It produces x_t from x_0 directly by scaling the data by \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)} and adding Gaussian noise of variance 1 - \bar\alpha(t).
Equivalently, in reparameterized form:  x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(t)}\, \epsilon  which lets us sample x_t for any t without iterating through the intermediate steps.

Marginal distribution p_t(x):

The perturbation kernel marginalized over x_0 \sim p_0 — the data-averaged marginal:  p_t(x) = \int p_{0t}(x \mid x_0)\, p_0(x_0)\, dx_0 
Whereas the perturbation kernel p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) conditions on a fixed x_0, the marginal averages over it, giving the unconditional law of x_t.


Scope: This post analyzes the forward process only — the object Itô’s lemma acts on. The reverse process, and the score \nabla_x \log p that drives it, are the subject of post #2. What we build here — the forward process’s continuous-time form and its perturbation kernels — is what the reverse process and its training will need.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
4.6 Assumptions
The forward process rests on a few modeling choices and collecting them upfront keeps the construction — and its limitations — transparent.

Standardized data: \mathbb{E}[x_0] = 0 and \operatorname{Var}(x_0) = I (the dataset is centered and whitened to meet this).
Prior p(x_N) / p(x_{t=1}): The schedule is chosen so that the noisiest state — x_N in discrete time, x_{t=1} in continuous time — is \approx \mathcal{N}(0, I), the fixed, data-independent distribution the reverse process starts from and the endpoint the construction is engineered to reach (not to be confused with a Bayesian prior).

These are idealizations: real data is only approximately standardized, and a finite number of steps leaves x_N only approximately Gaussian.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
4.7 The plan
With the objects defined and the assumptions fixed, the analysis of the forward process unfolds in three steps — the same Itô method of Parts 1–3, put to new questions:

Write the forward process as an SDE: The discrete noising sequence that defines DDPM is the discrete-time approximation of a continuous-time SDE. (Section 4.8)
Apply Itô’s lemma — twice:

Transform the SDE into the perturbation kernel: As an integrating-factor transform, Itô’s lemma collapses the drift and shows x_t \mid x_0 is Gaussian — the perturbation kernel, available in closed form, whose t \to 1 limit is the prior \mathcal{N}(0, I). (Section 4.9)
Derive the Fokker-Planck equation for the marginal distribution: Applied to a test function, Itô’s lemma gives the PDE governing the marginal distribution p_t(x). (Section 4.10)

Use the perturbation kernel for training: It lets us sample x_t for any t in a single step — what makes the DDPM training objective tractable. (Section 4.11)

These mirror the two roles Itô’s lemma played in Parts 2–3 — transforming an SDE and deriving a PDE — now being used for generation instead of option pricing.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
section: 4.8 The forward process as an SDE
text:
4.8 The forward process as an SDE
The DDPM forward process is defined in discrete time: a Markov chain — each state depending only on its immediate predecessor, not on the earlier history — that transports a data sample toward noise through a long sequence of small Gaussian noise additions, one per step:

\boxed{x_i = \sqrt{1 - \beta_i}\, x_{i-1} + \sqrt{\beta_i}\, \epsilon_i}
\tag{28}
where \beta_i is the discrete noise schedule and \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) is the independent noise injected at step i.
Song et al. [1] showed this discrete sequence is the Euler-Maruyama discretization of a continuous-time SDE [21] — the scheme that replaces dt by a step \Delta t and dW_t by an increment \Delta W_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Delta t\, I). To apply the Itô calculus to it, we must recover that SDE.
With that goal in mind, we first write the sequence explicitly, then let the step size shrink to zero to obtain the continuous-time limit. This yields an SDE of the same form as Equation 8, the Variance-Preserving SDE (VP-SDE), which exhibits the same drift-plus-diffusion structure as GBM.

4.8.1 The continuous-time form of the forward process
Partition the continuous interval [0, 1] into the N steps of even width \Delta t > 0:

0 = \tau_0 < \tau_1 < \cdots < \tau_N = 1, \qquad \tau_i = i\, \Delta t, \qquad \Delta t = \tfrac{1}{N}

Thus, continuous time \tau_i = i/N corresponds to step i. The step size \Delta t = 1/N \to 0 as N \to \infty.
We use the discrete noise schedule \beta_i = \beta(\tau_i)\, \Delta t, a function of \beta(t). To be able to apply the limit, from here we use the continuous time t in place of the grid point \tau_i i.e. \beta_i = \beta(t)\, \Delta t.
Substituting this into Equation 28, 
x_i = \sqrt{1 - \beta(t)\, \Delta t}\, x_{i-1} + \sqrt{\beta(t)\, \Delta t}\, \epsilon_i

For small \Delta t, Taylor-expanding the square root gives \sqrt{1 - \beta(t)\, \Delta t} \approx 1 - \tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, \Delta t,

x_i \;\approx\; \big(1 - \tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, \Delta t\big)\, x_{i-1} \;+\; \sqrt{\beta(t)\, \Delta t}\, \epsilon_i

Subtracting x_{i-1},

x_i - x_{i-1} \;\approx\; -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x_{i-1}\, \Delta t \;+\; \sqrt{\beta(t)\, \Delta t}\, \epsilon_i

Factoring the noise term as \sqrt{\beta(t)}\big(\sqrt{\Delta t}\, \epsilon_i\big),

x_i - x_{i-1} \;\approx\; -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x_{i-1}\, \Delta t \;+\; \sqrt{\beta(t)}\,\big(\sqrt{\Delta t}\, \epsilon_i\big)

The factor \sqrt{\Delta t}\, \epsilon_i, with \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), is exactly a Brownian increment \Delta W_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Delta t\, I) over [\tau_{i-1}, \tau_i],

x_i - x_{i-1} \;\approx\; -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x_{i-1}\, \Delta t \;+\; \sqrt{\beta(t)}\, \Delta W_i

This difference equation is the Euler-Maruyama scheme of the SDE below, and such schemes converge to the SDE’s solution as \Delta t \to 0 under the Lipschitz and linear-growth conditions of Section 2.1. Taking that limit gives the VP-SDE,

\boxed{dx_t = -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x_t\, dt + \sqrt{\beta(t)}\, dW_t}
\tag{29}
This is the continuous-time form of the DDPM forward process. \square


4.8.2 The structural parallel with GBM
Place the two SDEs side by side:

\begin{aligned}
\text{GBM (Black-Scholes stock):} \quad &dS_t = \mu S_t\, dt + \sigma S_t\, dW_t \\
\text{DDPM forward (VP-SDE):} \quad &dx_t = -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x_t\, dt + \sqrt{\beta(t)}\, dW_t
\end{aligned}

Both are linear SDEs: the drift is linear in the state variable, and the diffusion is either linear in the state variable (GBM) or independent of it (VP-SDE). The drift sign is the essential difference: GBM has a positive expected return (+\mu S), DDPM forward has a contracting drift (-\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t) x) that pulls x toward zero. Combined with the diffusion term injecting noise, this drives x_t toward a standard normal as t \to 1 (Figure 14).








Figure 14: Sample paths of GBM (left) and the VP-SDE (right), both starting at 1 (S_0 = 1 and x_0 = 1) and both linear SDEs driven by Brownian motion. GBM exhibits geometric drift. The VP-SDE pulls each path’s mean toward zero (dashed) while injecting noise, so the paths forget x_0 and settle into the unit-variance band \pm\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha(t)} \to \pm 1 (shaded): the law of x_t given x_0 approaches \mathcal{N}(0, 1), not a point.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
section: 4.9 Itô’s lemma derives the perturbation kernel
text:
4.9 Itô’s lemma derives the perturbation kernel
Here Itô’s lemma is applied as an integrating-factor transform: choosing the transform y_t = x_t / \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)} makes Itô’s lemma collapse the drift, turning the VP-SDE Equation 29 into a driftless process. Integrating that driftless process gives x_t \mid x_0 a closed-form Gaussian law — the perturbation kernel that is the central computational object of DDPM training.

4.9.1 Cumulative product \bar\alpha_i / \bar\alpha(t)
The discrete cumulative product of the factors 1 - \beta_j is:

\bar\alpha_i = \prod_{j=1}^{i}(1 - \beta_j)

Writing the product as the exponential of a log-sum,

\bar\alpha_i = \exp\!\big(\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{i}\log(1 - \beta_j)\big)

Using \log(1 - \beta_j) \approx -\beta_j for small \beta_j,

\bar\alpha_i \approx \exp\!\big(-\sum_{j=1}^{i}\beta_j\big)

Substituting the discrete schedule \beta_j = \beta(\tau_j)\, \Delta t, which makes the exponent a Riemann sum,

\bar\alpha_i \approx \exp\!\big(-\sum_{j=1}^{i}\beta(\tau_j)\, \Delta t\big)

Taking the continuum limit (N \to \infty, with t = i/N fixed), the Riemann sum becomes an integral,

\bar\alpha_i \to \exp\!\big(-\int_0^t \beta(s)\, ds\big)

which is the continuous cumulative product,

\boxed{\bar\alpha(t) = \exp\left(-\int_0^t \beta(s)\, ds\right)}
\tag{30}


4.9.2 Perturbation kernel p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0)
Because the VP-SDE is linear, it admits a closed-form solution: the law of x_t \mid x_0 for a fixed x_0. With the intermediate states integrated out, conditional on x_0, the state at time t is Gaussian:

\boxed{x_t \mid x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0,\ (1 - \bar\alpha(t)) I\right)}
\tag{31}
This perturbation kernel p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) lets us sample x_t for any t in a single step without simulating the SDE.


4.9.3 Derivation of the perturbation kernel
The derivation restates the SDE, defines an integrating factor and applies Itô’s lemma to it to eliminate the drift, integrates the driftless process, then inverts the transform.

4.9.3.1 Use Itô to get reduced SDE
The SDE: The state x_t follows the VP-SDE Equation 29,

dx_t \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x_t\, dt \;+\; \sqrt{\beta(t)}\, dW_t

Itô’s lemma: For a transform f(x_t, t) of a process with drift coefficient a and diffusion coefficient b — that is, dx_t = a\, dt + b\, dW_t — the lemma Equation 13 reads

df \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; a\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, b^2\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\right) dt \;+\; b\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dW

Integrating factor: Like OU, the standard technique for a linear SDE is to apply Itô’s lemma to the transform y_t = f(x_t, t) with f(x, t) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}}.
Coefficients (from the VP-SDE): a = -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x and b = \sqrt{\beta(t)}.
Partials (from f = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}}): With \bar\alpha'(t) = -\beta(t)\,\bar\alpha(t), which follows from differentiating Equation 30 by the chain rule,

\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;=\; \frac{x\,\beta(t)}{2\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}}, \qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}}, \qquad \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} \;=\; 0

Substituting a = -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x, b = \sqrt{\beta(t)}, and the three partials into the lemma,

dy_t \;=\; \left(\frac{x_t\, \beta(t)}{2\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}} \;+\; \left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x_t\right)\frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\,\beta(t)\cdot 0\right) dt \;+\; \sqrt{\beta(t)}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}}\, dW_t

Simplifying — the explicit-time term and the drift term cancel,

dy_t \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{\beta(t)}{\bar\alpha(t)}}\, dW_t

so y_t is driftless.


4.9.3.2 Solve reduced SDE by integration
Integrating both sides of the driftless equation from 0 to t,

\int_0^t dy_s \;=\; \int_0^t \sqrt{\frac{\beta(s)}{\bar\alpha(s)}}\, dW_s

Evaluating the left side by the fundamental theorem of calculus,

y_t - y_0 \;=\; \int_0^t \sqrt{\frac{\beta(s)}{\bar\alpha(s)}}\, dW_s

Since y_0 = x_0/\sqrt{\bar\alpha(0)} and \bar\alpha(0) = 1, y_0 = x_0; substituting,

y_t - x_0 \;=\; \int_0^t \sqrt{\frac{\beta(s)}{\bar\alpha(s)}}\, dW_s

Moving x_0 across,

y_t \;=\; x_0 \;+\; \int_0^t \sqrt{\frac{\beta(s)}{\bar\alpha(s)}}\, dW_s



4.9.3.3 Properties of the solution distribution
The Itô integral has a deterministic integrand g(s) = \sqrt{\dfrac{\beta(s)}{\bar\alpha(s)}}, so by Equation 7 it is Gaussian, with mean 0 and variance \int_0^t g(s)^2\, ds.
Conditioning on x_0, the offset x_0 is a deterministic constant; adding it to that Gaussian is an affine transformation, and an affine function of a Gaussian is Gaussian, hence

y_t \mid x_0 \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(x_0,\;\, \left(\int_0^t \frac{\beta(s)}{\bar\alpha(s)}\, ds\right) I\right)

Substituting \beta(s) = -\dfrac{\bar\alpha'(s)}{\bar\alpha(s)} (from \bar\alpha'(s) = -\beta(s)\,\bar\alpha(s)) into the variance,

y_t \mid x_0 \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(x_0,\;\, \left(\int_0^t \frac{-\bar\alpha'(s)}{\bar\alpha(s)^2}\, ds\right) I\right)

Recognizing the integrand as \dfrac{d}{ds}\!\left[\dfrac{1}{\bar\alpha(s)}\right],

y_t \mid x_0 \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(x_0,\;\, \left(\int_0^t \frac{d}{ds}\!\left[\frac{1}{\bar\alpha(s)}\right] ds\right) I\right)

Applying the fundamental theorem of calculus,

y_t \mid x_0 \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(x_0,\;\, \left(\frac{1}{\bar\alpha(t)} \;-\; \frac{1}{\bar\alpha(0)}\right) I\right)

Evaluating, with \bar\alpha(0) = 1,

y_t \mid x_0 \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(x_0,\;\, \frac{1 - \bar\alpha(t)}{\bar\alpha(t)}\, I\right)

Since x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, y_t,

\boxed{x_t \mid x_0 \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0,\;\, \big(1 - \bar\alpha(t)\big)\, I\right)}

which is Equation 31. \square


4.9.3.4 The terminal condition
The closed form delivers the endpoint the forward process was built to reach. Since \beta(s) > 0, the factor \bar\alpha(t) (Equation 30) decreases monotonically from \bar\alpha(0) = 1 toward 0 as the accumulated noise \int_0^t \beta(s)\, ds grows; the schedule is chosen so that \int_0^1 \beta(s)\, ds is large enough to make \bar\alpha(1) \approx 0.
Under that choice, evaluating Equation 31 at t = 1,

\mathbb{E}[x_{t=1} \mid x_0] = \sqrt{\bar\alpha(1)}\, x_0 \;\approx\; 0, \qquad \operatorname{Var}[x_{t=1} \mid x_0] = \big(1 - \bar\alpha(1)\big) I \;\approx\; I

Since Equation 31 is Gaussian, these moments give p_{01}(x_{t=1} \mid x_0) \approx \mathcal{N}(0, I) for every starting point x_0; the marginal is the average of that kernel over x_0 \sim p_0, so it inherits the same law. With the continuous endpoint t = 1 corresponding to the discrete step N,

\boxed{p(x_N) \;\approx\; \mathcal{N}(0, I)}
\tag{32}
The data x_0 is almost completely forgotten: every starting point flows to nearly the same standard Gaussian, the approximation tightening as \int_0^1 \beta\, ds is made larger (Figure 15). The idealized exact value \bar\alpha(1) = 0 is never attained on [0, 1]. It is approached only as the schedule’s total noise \int_0^1 \beta(s)\, ds grows without bound.








Figure 15: As t \to 1 the schedule drives \bar\alpha(t) toward 0: the mean factor \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)} (rose) decays toward 0, erasing the data’s contribution, while the variance 1 - \bar\alpha(t) (violet) rises toward 1. The perturbation kernel \mathcal{N}(\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\,x_0,\,(1-\bar\alpha(t))I) therefore approaches \mathcal{N}(0, I) for every starting point x_0 — the fixed prior the reverse process samples from. (Linear schedule \beta(t) from 0.1 to 20.)





This is the prior of Section 4.6, and it is what makes generation possible. To synthesize a sample, the reverse process starts from a sample from \mathcal{N}(0, I) (which is trivial to generate) and removes the noise; because the forward process lands every input on this one known distribution, the reverse process always has a fixed, data-independent place to begin.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
section: 4.10 Itô’s lemma derives the Fokker-Planck equation
text:
4.10 Itô’s lemma derives the Fokker-Planck equation
The perturbation kernel Equation 31 uses a fixed starting point x_0 and tracks the single conditioned state x_t \mid x_0. Here we take the more general perspective and ask how the marginal distribution p_t(x) — the full time-t density p(x, t) of the state — evolves. To answer that Itô’s lemma is applied to a smooth test function of the state, and the resulting identity is recast as a PDE for p(x, t).

4.10.1 Marginal distribution p_t(x)
The marginal distribution is the perturbation kernel Equation 31 marginalized over x_0 \sim p_0,

\boxed{p_t(x) = \int p_{0t}(x \mid x_0)\, p_0(x_0)\, dx_0}
\tag{33}
The two are different objects: the perturbation kernel fixes x_0, whereas the marginal distribution lets x_0 vary.

4.10.1.1 Why “Variance-Preserving”
The claim is about the variance of x_t under the marginal distribution, where both the data x_0 and the injected noise are random, so both contribute to its variance. The two terms of the reparameterized form x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(t)}\, \epsilon are independent, so their variances add. Taking the variance,

\operatorname{Var}(x_t) = \operatorname{Var}\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0\big) + \operatorname{Var}\big(\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(t)}\, \epsilon\big)

Taking each deterministic factor out of its variance, squared,

\operatorname{Var}(x_t) = \bar\alpha(t)\, \operatorname{Var}(x_0) + \big(1 - \bar\alpha(t)\big) \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon)

Substituting \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon) = I,

\operatorname{Var}(x_t) = \bar\alpha(t)\, \operatorname{Var}(x_0) + \big(1 - \bar\alpha(t)\big) I

With standardized data, \operatorname{Var}(x_0) = I,

\operatorname{Var}(x_t) = \bar\alpha(t)\, I + \big(1 - \bar\alpha(t)\big) I

Adding the two terms,

\operatorname{Var}(x_t) = I

So \operatorname{Var}(x_t) is constant for all t. As we add more and more noise in each step of the forward process, the data term’s variance \bar\alpha(t)\, I shrinks toward 0 and the noise term’s variance \big(1 - \bar\alpha(t)\big) I grows toward I but the total stays constant at I; hence the variance is preserved.
The variance of the perturbation kernel behaves differently. With x_0 fixed, the data term \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0 is a constant and contributes nothing; only the injected noise does, so Equation 31 has

\operatorname{Var}[x_t \mid x_0] = (1 - \bar\alpha(t))\, I

which is not constant — it grows toward I as more noise is added. So “Variance-Preserving” is a statement about the marginal distribution, not the perturbation kernel at fixed x_0.



4.10.2 Fokker-Planck equation
We state the result for a generic scalar SDE first, then specialize to the VP-SDE.
Write the process as X_t (capital, to mark it as the random state) with realized value x — the argument of its density p(x, t). Assume X_t has a density p(x, t) that is twice continuously differentiable in x and continuously differentiable in t, that \mu and \sigma are continuous with \mu p and \sigma^2 p twice continuously differentiable in x, and that \mathbb{E}\!\int_0^t \sigma(X_s, s)^2\, ds < \infty. For a generic SDE dX_t = \mu(X_t, t)\, dt + \sigma(X_t, t)\, dW_t, the density then satisfies the Fokker-Planck equation [22], [23]:

\boxed{\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} = -\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left[\mu(x, t)\, p(x, t)\right] + \frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}\left[\sigma^2(x, t)\, p(x, t)\right]}
\tag{34}
As \mu = -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x, \sigma = \sqrt{\beta(t)} for the VP-SDE,

\boxed{\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} = \frac{1}{2}\beta(t)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left[x\, p\right] + \frac{1}{2}\beta(t)\frac{\partial^2 p}{\partial x^2}}
\tag{35}
The second-order term has the same origin as the second-order term in the Black-Scholes PDE: it is the consequence of (dW)^2 = dt.


4.10.3 Derivation of Fokker-Planck equation
We derive both Equation 34 and Equation 35 now (see also [22]). The strategy is the weak formulation: rather than analyze p(x, t) directly, test it against an arbitrary smooth \varphi, take expectations to get rid of the dW_t term, then integrate by parts to move every derivative off \varphi and onto \mu p and \sigma^2 p — leaving an identity that must hold for all \varphi, which is the PDE.
Step 1 — Itô on a smooth test function:
Let \varphi: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} be a smooth function with compact support (i.e. \varphi \equiv 0 outside some bounded interval), so \varphi and all its derivatives vanish at the integration boundaries. Apply Itô’s lemma to \varphi(X_t) (no explicit t-dependence in \varphi):

d\varphi(X_t) \;=\; \left[\,\mu(X_t, t)\, \varphi'(X_t) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2(X_t, t)\, \varphi''(X_t)\,\right] dt \;+\; \sigma(X_t, t)\, \varphi'(X_t)\, dW_t

Step 2 — take expectations:
This differential is shorthand for its integral form; integrating from 0 to t,

\varphi(X_t) - \varphi(X_0) \;=\; \int_0^t \left[\,\mu\, \varphi' \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \varphi''\,\right] ds \;+\; \int_0^t \sigma\, \varphi'\, dW_s

Taking expectations of both sides,

\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_t)] - \mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_0)] \;=\; \mathbb{E}\!\int_0^t \left[\,\mu\, \varphi' \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \varphi''\,\right] ds \;+\; \mathbb{E}\!\int_0^t \sigma\, \varphi'\, dW_s

The last term is an Itô integral with zero expectation, by the martingale property proved for adapted integrands in Appendix A.4; its integrand \sigma\, \varphi' is bounded, since \varphi has compact support and \sigma is continuous, so the square-integrability that property requires holds. Dropping it,

\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_t)] - \mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_0)] \;=\; \mathbb{E}\!\int_0^t \left[\,\mu\, \varphi' \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \varphi''\,\right] ds

Interchanging the expectation and the time integral, which Fubini’s theorem permits because the integrand is bounded on [0, t],

\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_t)] - \mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_0)] \;=\; \int_0^t \mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\mu\, \varphi' \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \varphi''\,\right] ds

Differentiating in t (the lower limit and \mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_0)] are constant),

\frac{d}{dt}\, \mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_t)] \;=\; \mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\mu(X_t, t)\, \varphi'(X_t) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2(X_t, t)\, \varphi''(X_t)\,\right]

Writing each expectation as an integral against the density p(x, t),

\frac{d}{dt}\!\int \varphi(x)\, p(x, t)\, dx \;=\; \int \!\left[\,\mu(x, t)\, \varphi'(x) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2(x, t)\, \varphi''(x)\,\right] p(x, t)\, dx

Since \varphi is fixed and compactly supported and \partial p / \partial t is continuous, differentiation passes under the integral on the left, giving

\int \varphi(x)\, \frac{\partial p}{\partial t}\, dx \;=\; \int \!\left[\,\mu(x, t)\, \varphi'(x) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2(x, t)\, \varphi''(x)\,\right] p(x, t)\, dx

Step 3 — integrate by parts:
The goal is to move the derivatives off \varphi and onto \mu p and \sigma^2 p. The tool is integration by parts, whose full form over \mathbb{R} is

\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} u'\, v\, dx \;=\; \big[\, u\, v \,\big]_{-\infty}^{\infty} \;-\; \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} u\, v'\, dx

In every application below, u is \varphi or one of its derivatives, which becomes 0 at \pm\infty due to the compact support property; the boundary term [\,u v\,]_{-\infty}^{\infty} is thus 0, leaving the reduced rule

\int u'\, v\, dx \;=\; -\int u\, v'\, dx

Splitting the right side of Step 2 into its two terms,

\int \varphi(x)\, \frac{\partial p}{\partial t}\, dx \;=\; \int \mu\, \varphi'\, p\, dx \;+\; \int \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\, \varphi''\, p\, dx

Drift term: Applying the rule to the first term with u' = \varphi' and v = \mu p (so u = \varphi),

\int \varphi(x)\, \frac{\partial p}{\partial t}\, dx \;=\; -\int \varphi\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\!\big(\mu p\big)\, dx \;+\; \int \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\, \varphi''\, p\, dx

Diffusion term: The second term carries the second-order derivative of \varphi, so apply the rule twice. First with u' = \varphi'' and v = \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 p (so u = \varphi'),

\int \varphi(x)\, \frac{\partial p}{\partial t}\, dx \;=\; -\int \varphi\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\!\big(\mu p\big)\, dx \;-\; \int \varphi'\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\!\big(\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 p\big)\, dx

Applying it again with u' = \varphi' and v = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\big(\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 p\big) (so u = \varphi),

\int \varphi(x)\, \frac{\partial p}{\partial t}\, dx \;=\; -\int \varphi\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\!\big(\mu p\big)\, dx \;+\; \int \varphi\, \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}\!\big(\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 p\big)\, dx

Collecting under one integral,

\int \varphi(x)\, \frac{\partial p}{\partial t}\, dx \;=\; \int \varphi(x)\, \left[\,-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\!\big(\mu\, p\big) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}\!\big(\sigma^2\, p\big)\,\right] dx

Step 4 — match integrands:
Since this identity holds for every compactly-supported smooth test function \varphi, the two integrands must agree pointwise. This is the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations [24]: if \int g(x)\,\varphi(x)\, dx = 0 for all such \varphi, then g \equiv 0 — otherwise a bump function \varphi concentrated where g \neq 0 would make the integral nonzero. Thus, matching the integrands:

\boxed{\frac{\partial p}{\partial t}(x, t) \;=\; -\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\!\big[\mu(x, t)\, p(x, t)\big] \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}\!\big[\sigma^2(x, t)\, p(x, t)\big]}

which is Equation 34. \square


4.10.4 Specialization of Fokker-Planck equation to the VP-SDE
Substituting \mu(x, t) = -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x and \sigma^2(x, t) = \beta(t) into the Fokker-Planck equation Equation 34,

\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} \;=\; -\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\!\Big[\big(-\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x\big)\, p\Big] \;+\; \frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}\!\big[\beta(t)\, p\big]

As \beta(t) is independent of x,

\boxed{\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\!\big[x\, p\big] \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, \frac{\partial^2 p}{\partial x^2}}

which is Equation 35. \square
The Fokker-Planck perspective will become essential in post #3 when we discuss the reverse-time SDE, because the reverse process depends on \nabla_x \log p(x, t), which depends on the density p itself, not on simulated paths.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
4.11 Why the perturbation kernel matters
The perturbation kernel Equation 31 is what renders DDPM training tractable. Two consequences make this precise.
Constant-cost sampling: The reparameterized form of the perturbation kernel,

\boxed{x_t \;=\; \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0 \;+\; \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(t)}\, \epsilon}
\tag{36}
evaluates the state at any time t in closed form: given a noise-free sample x_0, a time t, and a single noise sample \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), the state x_t is obtained by one affine combination — at cost O(1) in t, with no iteration through the intermediate states between x_0 and x_t.
Exact supervision: Because \epsilon is sampled explicitly when x_t is constructed, the noise realized in x_t is known exactly. It therefore serves as a ground-truth regression target — the known quantity the network, observing only (x_t, t), is trained to predict.
Neither property survives the loss of the closed form. Recovering x_t at a time t would then require simulating the forward process — iterating the transition Equation 28, or an Euler-Maruyama step of the SDE, for \Theta(N) sequential steps per sample at every training iteration, against the closed form’s single O(1) evaluation, and with no available parallelism across steps. Moreover, the noise present in a simulated x_t is the cumulative effect of the per-step increments \epsilon_1, \ldots, \epsilon_i rather than a single \epsilon, so the exact regression target is no longer available. That target stands in for the score \nabla_x \log p_t. The perturbation kernel makes the conditional score a known multiple of the noise, \nabla_{x_t} \log p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) = -\epsilon / \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(t)}, and post #2 shows that regressing on it recovers \nabla_x \log p_t. Without the closed form neither is available, and the score must be estimated by other means, such as implicit score matching [18].
The perturbation kernel thus reduces training to single-step sampling with an exact, analytically known target. The use of that target — the denoising network, the noise-prediction objective, and its equivalence to score matching — concerns the reverse process and is developed in post #2. Part 4 establishes the object on which that construction depends.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
4.12 What the forward process establishes
Part 4 delivered, in sequence:

We started with a discrete sequence that drives a data sample toward pure noise.
Shrinking the step size gave an SDE for the state x_t — the VP-SDE.
Itô’s lemma, as an integrating-factor transform, collapsed its drift and made x_t \mid x_0 Gaussian — the perturbation kernel, in closed form.
At t = 1, that perturbation kernel is approximately \mathcal{N}(0, I) — the fixed, data-independent prior the reverse process starts from.
Itô’s lemma again — this time on a test function — gave the Fokker-Planck equation for how the full density p(x, t) evolves.
Because the perturbation kernel is closed-form, we can sample x_t in a single step, which is what makes the training objective tractable.

The \tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, \partial_x^2 p term in the Fokker-Planck equation Equation 35 is the trace of (dW)^2 = dt — the Itô correction carried into the density’s evolution. The next part places this construction alongside the Black-Scholes derivation to make the shared structure explicit.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
section: 6.1 Which room you walked in from
text:
6.1 Which room you walked in from
This correspondence — one lemma, one second-order correction, behind both option pricing and the diffusion forward process — is worth your effort, because it reads differently depending on where you come from. If you came up through machine learning, the finance side is a ready-made vocabulary for objects you reinvented; if you came up through quantitative finance, the diffusion side is, under new names, machinery you already hold. Pick your reading below.

6.1.1 For the machine-learning practitioner
The quantitative finance vocabulary is worth a week of your time. Almost every object you meet on the diffusion side has a quant name and a fifty-year head start: the VP-SDE is a time-dependent OU process — the same mean-reverting dynamics the Vasicek model [9] uses for interest rates; the closed-form perturbation kernel comes from the same integrating-factor transform we used to solve OU; and the -\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 volatility drag in the GBM log-return (Equation 15) is the same Itô correction appearing as the \tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\,\partial_x^2 p diffusion term in the forward process’s Fokker-Planck equation (Equation 35). What carries over is not any single formula but the habit it trains: moving fluently between an SDE and the PDE for its density, and between one sample path and the law it is sampled from.


6.1.2 For the quant
Diffusion models are closer than they look — re-application, not a pivot. If you can hedge an option, you already own the hard part: Itô’s lemma, the drift-plus-diffusion split, and the (dW)^2 = dt rule that keeps the second-order term alive. A diffusion model’s forward process is a linear SDE you would have recognized on sight, and deriving its perturbation kernel uses the same integrating-factor transform that solved OU in Section 2.4.2. What is genuinely new sits on top of the calculus, not underneath it: the question has changed from pricing a claim to generating a sample, and a neural network is introduced to learn one quantity classical pricing never needed — the score \nabla_x \log p. The machinery you would reach for is already in your hands.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
6.2 What comes next
I stopped here, deliberately, at the forward process — the easy direction: noise is added, with no need to train a model, and every conditional x_t \mid x_0 is a closed-form Gaussian. Generation is the hard direction — it must learn to undo that noise, and the distribution it needs is no longer a simple Gaussian but the unknown data distribution. It runs the dynamics backward in time, from pure noise to a sample. That reversal is the subject of posts #2 and #3 — the score \nabla_x \log p that drives it (post #2), the one quantity the forward analysis here never had to compute, and Anderson’s reverse-time SDE [26] (post #3).
Writing the forward process as an SDE was the first step. In post #3 that viewpoint becomes a general framework — the single equation that unifies the two lineages of diffusion modeling — and once a generative process lives as an SDE, that one representation opens a series of doors: flow matching, Langevin sampling, conditional generation, and the Variance-Exploding versus Variance-Preserving choice of forward SDE. Each is a later post, and each is a new question put to the machinery you now hold — Itô’s lemma and (dW)^2 = dt — applied to the SDE form that unifies everything to come.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
Appendix

A.1 Random walks and the Brownian limit
The Definition called Brownian motion the “continuum limit of a random walk.” This appendix makes that precise: it defines a random walk, applies the diffusive scaling, and shows the rescaled walk reproduces every defining property of Brownian motion in the limit.
The random walk: Let \xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots be independent, identically distributed steps with mean 0 and variance 1 — for concreteness, \pm 1 coin flips, though any such distribution works. The random walk after n steps is the partial sum

R_n \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^{n} \xi_k, \qquad R_0 = 0

By independence its variance is \operatorname{Var}(R_n) = n: the walk spreads like \sqrt{n}.
The diffusive scaling: To pack N steps into one unit of time we rescale time by 1/N and space by 1/\sqrt{N} — the \sqrt{N} is forced by the variance growing like the step count. Define the continuous, piecewise-linear process

W^{(N)}_t \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\, R_{\lfloor N t \rfloor}, \qquad t \in [0, 1]

(linearly interpolated between steps). As N \to \infty the steps shrink like 1/\sqrt{N} and arrive N to a unit interval — the limit the Definition invoked.
Matching Brownian motion’s properties: We verify the rescaled walk reproduces the four defining properties in the limit.
Starts at zero: W^{(N)}_0 = R_0/\sqrt{N} = 0 for every N — property 1, exactly.
Gaussian at each time: Fix t > 0 and write n = \lfloor N t \rfloor. Then

W^{(N)}_t = \frac{R_n}{\sqrt{N}}

Multiplying and dividing by \sqrt{n},

W^{(N)}_t = \sqrt{\tfrac{n}{N}}\;\cdot\;\frac{R_n}{\sqrt{n}}

Since n/N \to t and, by the central limit theorem (CLT), R_n/\sqrt{n} \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, 1),

W^{(N)}_t \;\xrightarrow{d}\; \sqrt{t}\,\cdot\,\mathcal{N}(0, 1) \;=\; \mathcal{N}(0, t)

matching W_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, t) — the s = 0 case of property 2.
Independent, stationary increments: At grid times s = j/N < t = m/N, the increment W^{(N)}_t - W^{(N)}_s is assembled from the steps \xi_k with j < k \le m — a block disjoint from the steps forming W^{(N)}_s — and disjoint blocks of i.i.d. steps are independent (property 3); at non-grid times the linear interpolation shares at most one straddling step, an overlap that vanishes as N \to \infty, and the same CLT argument applied to that block gives W^{(N)}_t - W^{(N)}_s \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, t - s), a law depending only on t - s — completing property 2 and supplying its stationarity.
Continuous paths: Each W^{(N)} is continuous by construction. That the limit has continuous sample paths — and that convergence holds for whole paths, not merely fixed-time marginals — is Donsker’s invariance principle, the functional central limit theorem [7]: the law of W^{(N)} on the space of continuous functions converges to the law of standard Brownian motion. Property 4, and the full process-level statement, follow.
All four properties hold in the limit: Brownian motion is the diffusive-scaling limit of a random walk. The 1/\sqrt{N} space scaling set against the 1/N time scaling is the same \sqrt{\Delta t}-against-\Delta t balance that, read forward, yields the quadratic-variation identity (dW)^2 = dt (Equation 3).


A.2 Solving the Black-Scholes PDE — heat-equation transform sketch
This appendix sketches the standard route from the Black-Scholes PDE Equation 19 to the closed-form formula Equation 27. The procedure converts the Black-Scholes PDE into the constant-coefficient heat equation, solves it with the Gaussian heat kernel, and transforms back. The treatment follows Wilmott, Howison and Dewynne [14].
Step 1 — change of variables:
Introduce dimensionless coordinates

x \;=\; \log\!\big(S/K\big), \qquad \tau \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\, (T - t)

and factor out an exponential prefactor,

V(S, t) \;=\; K\, e^{-\alpha x \,-\, \beta \tau}\, u(x, \tau)

with constants \alpha, \beta to be chosen below (local to this appendix — unrelated to the DDPM rate \beta(t) of Part 4). The terminal time t = T corresponds to \tau = 0.
Step 2 — choose \alpha, \beta to collapse the equation:
Substituting into Equation 19 and computing the partials gives, with the abbreviation k := 2r/\sigma^2, a PDE for u(x, \tau) that still carries first- and zeroth-order terms:

\frac{\partial u}{\partial \tau} \;=\; \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} \;+\; \big[(k - 1) - 2\alpha\big]\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \;+\; \big[\alpha^2 + (1 - k)\alpha - k + \beta\big]\, u

Setting both lower-order coefficients to zero — (k-1) - 2\alpha = 0 and \alpha^2 + (1-k)\alpha - k + \beta = 0 — forces

\alpha \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\,(k - 1), \qquad \beta \;=\; \tfrac{1}{4}\,(k + 1)^2

What remains is the dimensionless heat equation

\frac{\partial u}{\partial \tau} \;=\; \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} \quad \text{on } \mathbb{R} \times (0, \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 T]

Step 3 — initial condition:
At \tau = 0 (i.e. t = T), the call payoff \max(S - K, 0) = K\, \max(e^x - 1, 0) becomes

u(x, 0) \;=\; \max\!\Big(e^{(\alpha + 1) x} \,-\, e^{\alpha x},\;\, 0\Big)

nonzero for x > 0.
Step 4 — solve via the heat kernel:
The solution of \partial_\tau u = \partial_{xx} u with initial data u(\cdot, 0) is the convolution

u(x, \tau) \;=\; \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi \tau}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} u(y, 0)\; \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x - y)^2}{4\tau}\right) dy

Step 5 — evaluate the two Gaussian-tail integrals:
The initial data has two exponential terms, restricted to y > 0. Each contributes a Gaussian-times-half-line integral; completing the square in the exponent reduces each to a standard-normal CDF N(\cdot). The arithmetic yields

u(x, \tau) \;=\; e^{(\alpha + 1) x \,+\, (\alpha + 1)^2 \tau}\, N(d_1)
\;-\; e^{\alpha x \,+\, \alpha^2 \tau}\, N(d_2)

with d_1 = \frac{x}{\sqrt{2\tau}} + (\alpha + 1)\sqrt{2\tau} and d_2 = \frac{x}{\sqrt{2\tau}} + \alpha\sqrt{2\tau}, each affine in x with slope 1/\sqrt{2\tau}; the back-transform in Step 6 turns them into the familiar d_1, d_2 of Equation 27.
Step 6 — transform back to (S, t):
Multiply through by the prefactor K\, e^{-\alpha x - \beta \tau}. The exponential terms in u pair against e^{-\alpha x - \beta \tau} to yield S and K\, e^{-r(T - t)} factors respectively. Substituting x = \log(S/K), \tau = \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2(T - t) in d_1, d_2 produces

d_1 \;=\; \frac{\log(S/K) + (r + \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)(T - t)}{\sigma\sqrt{T - t}}, \qquad
d_2 \;=\; d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{T - t}

and the option value collapses to

V(S, t) \;=\; S\, N(d_1) \;-\; K\, e^{-r(T - t)}\, N(d_2)

which is Equation 27. (Two computations are omitted from this sketch and are standard: substituting the Step 1 ansatz into Equation 19 to obtain the constant-coefficient equation for u, and completing the square in each of the two half-line Gaussian integrals of Step 5 to reach the two normal CDFs. Both are carried out in full in [14].)
Alternative route — Feynman-Kac / risk-neutral expectation: The same formula can be derived without solving a PDE. The Feynman-Kac formula identifies the Black-Scholes PDE solution with a conditional expectation:

V(S, t) \;=\; e^{-r(T-t)}\, \mathbb{E}^Q\!\Big[\,\max(S_T - K,\, 0)\;\Big|\; S_t = S\,\Big]

where the stock evolves under the risk-neutral measure Q (under which the drift is replaced by r — the change of measure is constructed via Girsanov’s theorem). Under Q, the log-return \log(S_T / S_t) is normal — an immediate consequence of applying Itô’s lemma to \log S as in Section 2.4.1, but with \mu \to r. Computing the expectation by direct lognormal integration reproduces the same expression, the route taken in Hull’s chapter 15 appendix [27], with N(d_2) now interpretable as the risk-neutral exercise probability Q(S_T > K) [28]; N(d_1) is not a Q-probability but the option’s delta \partial V / \partial S. Girsanov’s theorem is developed in full in Appendix A.2 of post #3, with complete proofs in [7], [22]. That appendix serves the series twice: it gives an alternative, measure-theoretic route to the Black-Scholes formula, and it supplies the change of measure behind the reverse-time SDE of the diffusion posts.


A.3 The self-financing hedging portfolio
Section 3.6 wrote d\Pi_t = dV - \Delta_t\,dS_t for the portfolio \Pi_t = V - \Delta_t S_t. With a time-varying hedge ratio, expanding the product of the incremented factors — (\Delta_t + d\Delta_t)(S_t + dS_t) - \Delta_t S_t — gives the Itô product rule,

d(\Delta_t S_t) \;=\; \Delta_t\,dS_t \;+\; S_t\,d\Delta_t \;+\; d\Delta_t\,dS_t

so the marked value of \Pi_t changes by dV - \Delta_t\,dS_t - S_t\,d\Delta_t - d\Delta_t\,dS_t — two terms beyond what the main derivation used. They drop out once the hedge is run as a self-financing strategy rather than bought and held.
Make the cash explicit: hold the option, short \Delta_t shares, and a risk-free cash account C_t earning rate r,

\Pi_t \;=\; V_t \;-\; \Delta_t S_t \;+\; C_t

Self-financing means every rebalance is paid from within the portfolio — no external cash in or out. Increasing the short by d\Delta_t releases S_t\,d\Delta_t + d\Delta_t\,dS_t of cash, so

dC_t \;=\; \underbrace{r\,C_t\,dt}_{\text{interest}} \;+\; \underbrace{S_t\,d\Delta_t + d\Delta_t\,dS_t}_{\text{cash from re-hedging}}

Taking the differential of the portfolio value,

d\Pi_t \;=\; dV_t \;-\; d(\Delta_t S_t) \;+\; dC_t

Substituting d(\Delta_t S_t) = \Delta_t\,dS_t + S_t\,d\Delta_t + d\Delta_t\,dS_t,

d\Pi_t \;=\; dV_t \;-\; \big(\Delta_t\,dS_t + S_t\,d\Delta_t + d\Delta_t\,dS_t\big) \;+\; dC_t

Substituting dC_t = r\,C_t\,dt + \big(S_t\,d\Delta_t + d\Delta_t\,dS_t\big),

d\Pi_t \;=\; dV_t \;-\; \big(\Delta_t\,dS_t + S_t\,d\Delta_t + d\Delta_t\,dS_t\big) \;+\; r\,C_t\,dt \;+\; \big(S_t\,d\Delta_t + d\Delta_t\,dS_t\big)

The re-hedging terms S_t\,d\Delta_t + d\Delta_t\,dS_t cancel,

d\Pi_t \;=\; dV_t \;-\; \Delta_t\,dS_t \;+\; r\,C_t\,dt

The no-arbitrage condition d\Pi_t = r\, \Pi_t\, dt applies to this riskless portfolio. Substituting \Pi_t = V_t - \Delta_t S_t + C_t on the right,

dV_t \;-\; \Delta_t\,dS_t \;+\; r\,C_t\,dt \;=\; r\,\big(V_t - \Delta_t S_t\big)\,dt \;+\; r\,C_t\,dt

Cancelling the r\,C_t\,dt terms on both sides,

dV_t \;-\; \Delta_t\,dS_t \;=\; r\,\big(V_t - \Delta_t S_t\big)\,dt

This is the relation the main derivation used, and it holds for every cash balance C_t. The -S_t\,d\Delta_t - d\Delta_t\,dS_t terms are not neglected; they are paid for by the cash leg.


A.4 The Itô integral, constructed
The main text (Section 1.8) used the fact that an Itô integral of a deterministic integrand is Gaussian, with a variance fixed by the Itô isometry. This appendix constructs the integral \int_0^T H_s\, dW_s for adapted, random integrands and proves the isometry it rests on, following Itô’s original construction [29], [30]. The non-anticipating requirement invoked below is made precise in Appendix A.5.
Step 1 — simple integrands:
Call H simple if it is piecewise constant on a partition 0 = t_0 < t_1 < \cdots < t_n = T, with H_s = \xi_i for s \in [t_i, t_{i+1}) and each \xi_i square-integrable and measurable with respect to the information available at t_i (it may depend on the path up to t_i, never beyond). For such H define the integral as the obvious sum:

\int_0^T H_s\, dW_s \;:=\; \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \xi_i \,\big(W_{t_{i+1}} - W_{t_i}\big)

Each increment \Delta W_i = W_{t_{i+1}} - W_{t_i} is independent of \xi_i (which is fixed by time t_i), with mean 0 and variance t_{i+1} - t_i.
Step 2 — the Itô isometry for simple integrands:
Taking the expected square and expanding,

\mathbb{E}\Big[\Big(\textstyle\sum_i \xi_i\, \Delta W_i\Big)^2\Big] = \sum_i \mathbb{E}\big[\xi_i^2\, (\Delta W_i)^2\big] + \sum_{i \ne j} \mathbb{E}\big[\xi_i\, \xi_j\, \Delta W_i\, \Delta W_j\big]

The cross terms vanish because increments over disjoint intervals are independent and mean-zero, and \xi_i is known by t_i,

\mathbb{E}\Big[\Big(\textstyle\sum_i \xi_i\, \Delta W_i\Big)^2\Big] = \sum_i \mathbb{E}\big[\xi_i^2\, (\Delta W_i)^2\big]

Substituting \mathbb{E}[(\Delta W_i)^2] = \Delta t_i (\Delta W_i independent of \xi_i),

\mathbb{E}\Big[\Big(\textstyle\sum_i \xi_i\, \Delta W_i\Big)^2\Big] = \sum_i \mathbb{E}\big[\xi_i^2\big]\,\Delta t_i

Recognizing the right side as the integral of the simple process H^2,

\mathbb{E}\Big[\Big(\textstyle\sum_i \xi_i\, \Delta W_i\Big)^2\Big] = \mathbb{E}\!\int_0^T H_s^2\, ds

That is the Itô isometry,

\boxed{\;\mathbb{E}\Big[\Big(\textstyle\int_0^T H_s\, dW_s\Big)^2\Big] \;=\; \mathbb{E}\!\int_0^T H_s^2\, ds\;}
\tag{37}
— the integral preserves the L^2 norm.
Step 3 — extension to general integrands:
For any adapted H with \mathbb{E}\!\int_0^T H_s^2\, ds < \infty, choose simple processes H^{(n)} \to H in L^2. By the isometry Equation 37 the integrals \int H^{(n)}\, dW form a Cauchy sequence in L^2(\Omega), which is complete, so they converge to a limit that does not depend on the approximating sequence. Define \int_0^T H_s\, dW_s as that limit. The isometry passes to the limit, so it holds for every such H.
Step 4 — the integral is a martingale:
For simple H and s \le t, \mathbb{E}\big[\int_0^t H\, dW \mid \mathcal{F}_s\big] = \int_0^s H\, dW — \mathcal{F}_s being the information available at time s, made precise in Appendix A.5 — because the increments after s have conditional mean zero. The property survives the L^2 limit, so M_t := \int_0^t H_s\, dW_s is a martingale with \mathbb{E}[M_t] = 0: it has no drift. This is the precise sense in which a dW term carries no trend.
Step 5 — connection to the main text:
When H_s = h(s) is deterministic, the integral is a limit of sums of independent Gaussians, hence itself Gaussian (Appendix A.6), with mean 0 and — by Equation 37 — variance \int_0^T h(s)^2\, ds. That is the statement used in Section 1.8. The infinitesimal shadow of the isometry, \mathbb{E}[(dW)^2] = dt, is the (dW)^2 = dt rule of the main text; quadratic variation is the same fact seen pathwise.
A construction at this level of detail is standard; see [7], [22].


A.5 Filtrations, adapted processes, and martingales
The two constructions above rely on a notion of “information available at time t” and on the integrand not peeking into the future. This appendix collects that scaffolding and makes precise the phrase used throughout — that a dW term is a martingale and so carries no drift.
Filtration: On a probability space (\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P}), a filtration (\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \ge 0} is an increasing family of \sigma-algebras, \mathcal{F}_s \subseteq \mathcal{F}_t for s \le t. Read \mathcal{F}_t as everything observable up to time t. For Brownian motion the natural choice is \mathcal{F}_t = \sigma(W_s : s \le t), the information generated by the path so far.
Adapted / non-anticipating: A process H_t is adapted if H_t is \mathcal{F}_t-measurable for every t — its value at t depends only on information up to t, never on the future. This is the requirement placed on Itô integrands in Appendix A.4, and it is not cosmetic: evaluating the integrand at the left endpoint t_i of each interval — so it cannot see the increment \Delta W_i it multiplies — is what makes the cross terms vanish, delivers the Itô isometry, and yields a martingale. Evaluating at the midpoint instead gives the Stratonovich integral [31], with an extra drift term and the ordinary chain rule — a different calculus.
Martingale: An adapted, integrable process M_t is a martingale if

\mathbb{E}[\, M_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s \,] = M_s \qquad (s \le t)

i.e. the best forecast of a future value, given the present, is the present value — no expected drift. Brownian motion is a martingale, and by Appendix A.4 so is the Itô integral \int_0^t H_s\, dW_s. (Conditional expectation \mathbb{E}[\,\cdot \mid \mathcal{F}_s\,] is the L^2-orthogonal projection onto \mathcal{F}_s-measurable variables — the least-squares forecast given the present.)
Why this underlies Itô’s lemma: Itô’s lemma writes a transformed process as

df(X_t, t) = \underbrace{\big(\partial_t f + \mu\, \partial_x f + \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\, \partial_{xx} f\big)\, dt}_{\text{drift}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sigma\, \partial_x f\, dW_t}_{\text{martingale part}}

The dW term is a martingale increment: conditioned on the present it has mean zero. Taking expectations therefore annihilates it and leaves only the drift — the step used (often silently) whenever the main text computes a mean, derives a moment equation, or passes from an SDE to the Fokker-Planck equation. “A martingale has no drift” is the statement that the dW part contributes nothing to the expected change.
These three notions — filtration, adapted integrand, martingale — are the measure-theoretic scaffolding beneath the heuristic (dW)^2 = dt calculus of the main text. For complete treatments see [7], [22].


A.6 Gaussian limits in L^2
Section 1.8 built the Itô integral as an L^2 limit of Gaussian partition sums and asserted that the limit is itself Gaussian. This appendix proves that closure fact.
Claim: Let X_n \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_n, \sigma_n^2) and suppose X_n \to X in L^2, i.e. \mathbb{E}[(X_n - X)^2] \to 0. Then \mu_n and \sigma_n^2 converge, and X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) with \mu = \lim_n \mu_n and \sigma^2 = \lim_n \sigma_n^2.
Step 1 — the moments pass to the limit:
By linearity of expectation,

|\mu_n - \mathbb{E}[X]| \;=\; \big|\mathbb{E}[X_n - X]\big|

By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality \mathbb{E}|YZ| \le \sqrt{\mathbb{E}[Y^2]}\,\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[Z^2]}, with Z = 1,

|\mu_n - \mathbb{E}[X]| \;\le\; \sqrt{\mathbb{E}[(X_n - X)^2]}

By the L^2 hypothesis the right-hand side tends to zero,

|\mu_n - \mathbb{E}[X]| \;\xrightarrow{\;n \to \infty\;}\; 0

so \mu_n \to \mu := \mathbb{E}[X]. For the second moment, expanding X_n = (X_n - X) + X,

\mathbb{E}[X_n^2] \;=\; \mathbb{E}[(X_n - X)^2] \;+\; 2\,\mathbb{E}[(X_n - X)\,X] \;+\; \mathbb{E}[X^2]

The first term vanishes by assumption, and the cross term is bounded by Cauchy-Schwarz, |\mathbb{E}[(X_n - X)\,X]| \le \sqrt{\mathbb{E}[(X_n - X)^2]}\,\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[X^2]} \to 0, so \mathbb{E}[X_n^2] \to \mathbb{E}[X^2] and therefore \sigma_n^2 = \mathbb{E}[X_n^2] - \mu_n^2 \to \mathbb{E}[X^2] - \mu^2 = \operatorname{Var}(X) =: \sigma^2.
Step 2 — X_n \to X in distribution:
L^2 convergence implies convergence in probability: since \mathbf{1}_{\{|Y| > \epsilon\}} \le Y^2 / \epsilon^2 pointwise, taking expectations gives

\mathbb{P}\big(|X_n - X| > \epsilon\big) \;\le\; \frac{\mathbb{E}[(X_n - X)^2]}{\epsilon^2} \;\xrightarrow{\;n \to \infty\;}\; 0

Convergence in probability in turn implies convergence of the distribution functions at continuity points: the event \{X_n \le x\} is contained in \{X \le x + \epsilon\} \cup \{|X_n - X| > \epsilon\}, and \{X \le x - \epsilon\} is contained in \{X_n \le x\} \cup \{|X_n - X| > \epsilon\}, so

\mathbb{P}(X \le x - \epsilon) - \mathbb{P}\big(|X_n - X| > \epsilon\big) \;\le\; \mathbb{P}(X_n \le x) \;\le\; \mathbb{P}(X \le x + \epsilon) + \mathbb{P}\big(|X_n - X| > \epsilon\big)

Letting n \to \infty and then \epsilon \to 0, at every continuity point x of the distribution function of X, \mathbb{P}(X_n \le x) \to \mathbb{P}(X \le x).
Step 3 — identify the limit law:
Suppose \sigma > 0. For every n large enough that \sigma_n > 0, which is all but finitely many since \sigma_n \to \sigma > 0, the distribution function of X_n is N\!\big((x - \mu_n)/\sigma_n\big), with N(\cdot) the standard normal CDF of Section 3.7.1. Since \mu_n \to \mu and \sigma_n \to \sigma > 0 (Step 1) and N is continuous,

N\!\left(\frac{x - \mu_n}{\sigma_n}\right) \;\xrightarrow{\;n \to \infty\;}\; N\!\left(\frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\right) \quad \text{for every } x

Step 2 gives the same sequence the limit \mathbb{P}(X \le x) at continuity points, and limits are unique, so \mathbb{P}(X \le x) = N\!\big((x - \mu)/\sigma\big) at every continuity point of the left side; both sides are non-decreasing and the right side is continuous everywhere, so the two agree for all x. That is, X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2).
The degenerate case \sigma = 0: Step 1 gives \operatorname{Var}(X) = 0 and \mathbb{E}[X] = \mu, so X = \mu almost surely — the constant limit, consistent with reading \mathcal{N}(\mu, 0) as a point mass.
Applied to Section 1.8: the partition sums are Gaussian with \mu_n = 0 and \sigma_n^2 = \sum_i g(t_i)^2\, \Delta t_i \to \int_0^t g(s)^2\, ds, and they converge in L^2 to the integral, so the integral is \mathcal{N}\big(0, \int_0^t g(s)^2\, ds\big) — which is Equation 7. \square For the general theory see [22].


A.7 Composing the forward transitions: the discrete perturbation kernel
The Definitions of Part 4 assert that composing the forward transitions p(x_i \mid x_{i-1}) = \mathcal{N}\big(x_i;\ \sqrt{1 - \beta_i}\, x_{i-1},\ \beta_i I\big) and marginalizing out the intermediate states yields the discrete perturbation kernel of DDPM [2],

p(x_i \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\!\big(x_i;\ \sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}\, x_0,\ (1 - \bar\alpha_i)\, I\big)

This appendix derives it by induction on i, working in the reparameterized form x_i = \sqrt{\alpha_i}\, x_{i-1} + \sqrt{\beta_i}\, \epsilon_i with \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) independent across steps.
Base case i = 1: The kernel is the first transition: x_1 = \sqrt{\alpha_1}\, x_0 + \sqrt{\beta_1}\, \epsilon_1, and since \bar\alpha_1 = \alpha_1 and \beta_1 = 1 - \alpha_1 = 1 - \bar\alpha_1, this is x_1 = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_1}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_1}\, \epsilon_1 — the claimed form.
Induction step: Assume the claim at step i-1: x_{i-1} = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_{i-1}}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_{i-1}}\, \bar\epsilon, where \bar\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) collects the noise of steps 1, \dots, i-1 and is therefore independent of the fresh step-i noise \epsilon_i. Substituting the induction hypothesis into the reparameterized transition,

x_i \;=\; \sqrt{\alpha_i}\left(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{i-1}}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_{i-1}}\, \bar\epsilon\right) + \sqrt{\beta_i}\, \epsilon_i

Expanding,

x_i \;=\; \sqrt{\alpha_i \bar\alpha_{i-1}}\, x_0 \;+\; \sqrt{\alpha_i (1 - \bar\alpha_{i-1})}\, \bar\epsilon \;+\; \sqrt{\beta_i}\, \epsilon_i

Combining the two independent zero-mean Gaussian noise terms into a single \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) — a linear combination of independent Gaussians is Gaussian and their variances add, the fact used for the partition sums of Section 1.8,

x_i \;=\; \sqrt{\alpha_i \bar\alpha_{i-1}}\, x_0 \;+\; \sqrt{\alpha_i (1 - \bar\alpha_{i-1}) + \beta_i}\, \epsilon

Substituting \beta_i = 1 - \alpha_i,

x_i \;=\; \sqrt{\alpha_i \bar\alpha_{i-1}}\, x_0 \;+\; \sqrt{\alpha_i (1 - \bar\alpha_{i-1}) + 1 - \alpha_i}\, \epsilon

Expanding the product under the square root — the \pm\alpha_i cancel,

x_i \;=\; \sqrt{\alpha_i \bar\alpha_{i-1}}\, x_0 \;+\; \sqrt{1 - \alpha_i \bar\alpha_{i-1}}\, \epsilon

Recognizing the cumulative product \bar\alpha_i = \alpha_i \bar\alpha_{i-1},

x_i \;=\; \sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}\, x_0 \;+\; \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_i}\, \epsilon

which is the claimed form at step i, so the induction closes: p(x_i \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\big(x_i;\ \sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}\, x_0,\ (1 - \bar\alpha_i)\, I\big) for every i. \square

title: Continuous-Time Generative Models
text:
This is a working series on the continuous-time stochastic-process family that underlies modern generative AI — diffusion models, score-based SDEs, flow matching, Langevin sampling, and conditional generation — explained by someone who used the same toolkit in quantitative finance. Each topic is derived rather than described. Note: it doesn’t cover other families like autoregressive models, GANs, or masked-token methods.



Posts






Date



Title








Sep 10, 2026


The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion






Aug 10, 2026


Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models






No matching items

I used to work in quantitative finance, but when generative AI began reshaping whole industries I grew curious enough to investigate how the new models worked. The deeper I went, the more I kept meeting old friends wearing new names. The “forward process” in a diffusion paper was an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process used for modeling interest rates. The same paper’s “reverse process”, which generates the image, can be derived by Girsanov’s theorem [1] — the same \mathbb{P}\to\mathbb{Q} change of measure that sits underneath every option price. The vocabularies had diverged; the mathematics had not. What was new was the application, not the machinery — a familiar toolkit aimed at a new field.
Digging into why the two lined up so neatly, I found that none of it began in either field. It started with Robert Brown in 1827, watching particles released from pollen grains jitter under a microscope and publishing the account the next year [2]. Einstein explained the jitter in 1905 [3]; Norbert Wiener made it rigorous in the 1920s as the Wiener process [4]. Kiyosi Itô then built stochastic calculus in the 1940s [5]: a chain rule for random paths (Itô’s lemma) and integration against Brownian motion. Its analytic twins, the Fokker-Planck equation [6], [7] for how a density evolves and the Feynman-Kac formula [8] linking such partial differential equations (PDEs) to expectations, complete the picture. Both finance and generative AI are downstream of physicists and mathematicians who were thinking about neither.
Finance borrowed it early. Louis Bachelier modeled stock prices as Brownian motion in 1900 [9] — five years before Einstein’s paper — though it sat ignored for decades. Real adoption came in 1973, when Black, Scholes, and Merton [10], [11] priced options by modeling the stock as geometric Brownian motion and applying Itô’s lemma to a hedged portfolio; the resulting PDE solves, via Feynman-Kac, to an expected discounted payoff. From there it spread: the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process [12] became the Vasicek model [13] of mean-reverting rates, and the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation the backbone of optimal portfolio choice [14]. A quant lives inside stochastic differential equations (SDEs) and PDE-expectation duality daily, rarely calling them by their physics names.
Diffusion models are borrowing it now. A generator defines a forward process that turns data into noise, then learns to run it backward. Song and colleagues’ 2021 framework [15] wrote this as an SDE; Anderson’s 1982 result [16] on reverse-time diffusions shows the generative process is that SDE run backward, driven by the score, the gradient of the log density. The most common forward choice, the Variance-Preserving SDE, is a time-dependent Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process; the marginal distribution evolves by Fokker-Planck. A quant reading this is not learning new mathematics, but recognizing familiar territory.
That is why the crossing is easy both ways. The core skill is identical: fluency with stochastic processes and Itô calculus, the instinct to move between an SDE and its PDE, and a feel for how probability flows under drift plus diffusion. A quant who knows why a martingale has no drift and how to discretize an SDE for Monte Carlo already owns the hard part of diffusion; an AI researcher who has tuned samplers and reasoned about score matching has practiced the continuous-time skills at the heart of quantitative finance. The new material on each side is real but learnable, sitting atop a shared core.
So here is my case to both rooms. The barrier is lexical, not conceptual: “risk-neutral drift” and “reverse-time drift” are two names for one operation, reshaping the drift by a change of measure, so each field keeps rediscovering what the other knows. Ideas already migrate both ways, but only the hard way — through specialists who stay in one field and learn the other’s dialect to do the work. Bühler, Teichmann and colleagues pulled the neural network, a tool born in AI, into derivatives hedging [17]; Wang, Zariphopoulou and Zhou carried stochastic optimal control, central to quantitative finance, into the AI problem of reinforcement learning [18]. That it works at all is the point: it works because the mathematics is already shared. It could happen far more readily, and by design. The wall between you is thinner than it looks, and some of the best ideas you could borrow are already sitting on the other side.
Post 1 builds the machinery the rest of the series runs on. It starts from Brownian motion and the single new rule (dW)^2 = dt, then develops Itô’s lemma from first principles. It turns that lemma, unchanged, on two problems half a century apart. The first is the Black-Scholes equation, reached through a hedged portfolio and no-arbitrage. The second is diffusion’s forward process, recast as the Variance-Preserving SDE with its perturbation kernel and Fokker-Planck equation. Quantitative finance and generative AI, it turns out, share an ancestor.
Post 2 crosses fully to generative AI and follows the two lineages of diffusion modeling. It takes the variational path first, through DDPM’s reverse process, the ELBO, and ancestral sampling. This is a working series on the continuous-time stochastic-process family that underlies modern generative AI — diffusion models, score-based SDEs, flow matching, Langevin sampling, and conditional generation — explained by someone who used the same toolkit in quantitative finance. Each topic is derived rather than described. Note: it doesn’t cover other families like autoregressive models, GANs, or masked-token methods.

Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models






No matching items

I used to work in quantitative finance, but when generative AI began reshaping whole industries I grew curious enough to investigate how the new models worked. The deeper I went, the more I kept meeting old friends wearing new names. The “forward process” in a diffusion paper was an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process used for modeling interest rates. The same paper’s “reverse process”, which generates the image, can be derived by Girsanov’s theorem [1] — the same \mathbb{P}\to\mathbb{Q} change of measure that sits underneath every option price. The vocabularies had diverged; the mathematics had not. What was new was the application, not the machinery — a familiar toolkit aimed at a new field.
Digging into why the two lined up so neatly, I found that none of it began in either field. It started with Robert Brown in 1827, watching particles released from pollen grains jitter under a microscope and publishing the account the next year [2]. Einstein explained the jitter in 1905 [3]; Norbert Wiener made it rigorous in the 1920s as the Wiener process [4]. Kiyosi Itô then built stochastic calculus in the 1940s [5]: a chain rule for random paths (Itô’s lemma) and integration against Brownian motion. Its analytic twins, the Fokker-Planck equation [6], [7] for how a density evolves and the Feynman-Kac formula [8] linking such partial differential equations (PDEs) to expectations, complete the picture. Both finance and generative AI are downstream of physicists and mathematicians who were thinking about neither.
Finance borrowed it early. Louis Bachelier modeled stock prices as Brownian motion in 1900 [9] — five years before Einstein’s paper — though it sat ignored for decades. Real adoption came in 1973, when Black, Scholes, and Merton [10], [11] priced options by modeling the stock as geometric Brownian motion and applying Itô’s lemma to a hedged portfolio; the resulting PDE solves, via Feynman-Kac, to an expected discounted payoff. From there it spread: the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process [12] became the Vasicek model [13] of mean-reverting rates, and the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation the backbone of optimal portfolio choice [14]. A quant lives inside stochastic differential equations (SDEs) and PDE-expectation duality daily, rarely calling them by their physics names.
Diffusion models are borrowing it now. A generator defines a forward process that turns data into noise, then learns to run it backward. Song and colleagues’ 2021 framework [15] wrote this as an SDE; Anderson’s 1982 result [16] on reverse-time diffusions shows the generative process is that SDE run backward, driven by the score, the gradient of the log density. The most common forward choice, the Variance-Preserving SDE, is a time-dependent Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process; the marginal distribution evolves by Fokker-Planck. A quant reading this is not learning new mathematics, but recognizing familiar territory.
That is why the crossing is easy both ways. The core skill is identical: fluency with stochastic processes and Itô calculus, the instinct to move between an SDE and its PDE, and a feel for how probability flows under drift plus diffusion. A quant who knows why a martingale has no drift and how to discretize an SDE for Monte Carlo already owns the hard part of diffusion; an AI researcher who has tuned samplers and reasoned about score matching has practiced the continuous-time skills at the heart of quantitative finance. The new material on each side is real but learnable, sitting atop a shared core.
So here is my case to both rooms. The barrier is lexical, not conceptual: “risk-neutral drift” and “reverse-time drift” are two names for one operation, reshaping the drift by a change of measure, so each field keeps rediscovering what the other knows. Ideas already migrate both ways, but only the hard way — through specialists who stay in one field and learn the other’s dialect to do the work. Bühler, Teichmann and colleagues pulled the neural network, a tool born in AI, into derivatives hedging [17]; Wang, Zariphopoulou and Zhou carried stochastic optimal control, central to quantitative finance, into the AI problem of reinforcement learning [18]. That it works at all is the point: it works because the mathematics is already shared. It could happen far more readily, and by design. The wall between you is thinner than it looks, and some of the best ideas you could borrow are already sitting on the other side.
Post 1 builds the machinery the rest of the series runs on. It starts from Brownian motion and the single new rule (dW)^2 = dt, then develops Itô’s lemma from first principles. It turns that lemma, unchanged, on two problems half a century apart. The first is the Black-Scholes equation, reached through a hedged portfolio and no-arbitrage. The second is diffusion’s forward process, recast as the Variance-Preserving SDE with its perturbation kernel and Fokker-Planck equation. Quantitative finance and generative AI, it turns out, share an ancestor.
Post 2 crosses fully to generative AI and follows the two lineages of diffusion modeling. It takes the variational path first, through DDPM’s reverse process, the ELBO, and ancestral sampling. It then builds the score-based path from first principles, covering the score, score matching in its explicit, implicit, and denoising forms, Vincent’s theorem and Tweedie’s formula, and the noise-conditional score networks and annealed Langevin dynamics that made score-based sampling work on real data. It closes by weighing what the reformulation from densities to scores bought, and hands both lineages to post 3.
